newsitem.title: USA: TENNIS-WOODBRIDGE ADVANCES WHEN CHESNOKOV INJURED, CASH LOSES.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-WOODBRIDGE ADVANCES WHEN CHESNOKOV INJURED, CASH LOSES.

text.p: Sixth-seeded Todd Woodbridge, one of five Australians but the only seed in action Tuesday, won an abbreviated first-round match Tuesday at the $714,250 Advanta Championships when Andrei Chesnokov of Russia broke his leg in a horrific oncourt accident.
Trailing 6-3 1-0, the unseeded, 69th-ranked Chesnokov, 31, broke his tibia and fibula and dislocated the ankle as he went for a backhand. He was to have surgery Wednesday at a local hospital.

Fellow Australian Patrick Rafter joined Woodbridge in the second round after scoring a 6-2 6-2 victory over countryman Mark Woodforde but Richard Fromberg failed to move on in the draw, falling to Byron Black of Zimbabwe 6-4 6-3, and former Wimbledon champion Pat Cash also let the Australian side down.
Ranked 489th in the world, the 31-year-old Cash, given a wildcard here, lost 6-4 6-0 to 38th-ranked Jonas Bjorkman of Sweden.

Since his dramatic 1987 Wimbledon triumph, Cash has struggled and sat out a number of years because of a series of medcal traumas. Since the beginning of 1996, Cash has played only seven matches for a 1-6 win-loss record.

"I want to give myself a chance to play some more because I like playing," Cash said. " I think if I had had the chance to play well and play a lot of matches, I would be quite happy to stop playing at this age."

Cash stayed with Bjorkman until the ninth game of the first set when he sailed a backhand wide on the third break point of the game. Bjorkman, who won his first career tournament in Auckland this January, won the final nine games of the match.
Without directly blaming the court for Chesnokov's injury, Cash and Woodbridge both criticised the surface here.
"This court is very slow and it's actually quite dangerous," said Cash. "It sticks and you can't move that well."
"This court is slow and you stick to the court quite a bit," said the 26th-ranked Woodbridge. "I don't think it's the court's fault that his ankle snapped in half but it is very sticky."
"It's the worst injury I've seen in tennis," said ATP Tour trainer Doug Spreen. "It's not a career-threatening type of injury, but I think he'll be out a minimum of four to six months."
